evidence_quotes.quote: firstly, residential water supply through networked of polymerizing vinyl chloride (PVC) pipes mostly to residents, who can afford the cost of networked water extension (Wamuchiru 2017), and secondly, served other residents who could not afford the metered water connection, through the everyday operations and selling of the water.

According to the Ubungo municipal water engineer, the following formal procedures are required before engaging in the water supply: Firstly, residents are required to register with the municipal council before water supply; secondly, obtain permission from DAWASA; and thirdly, obtain operation permit from the Ministry of Health (MoH). Unfortunately, only the public tanker trucks were registered. However, the municipal water engineer described the actions of the non-registered operators as a “survival strategy” but not as “criminal or illegal act.”

For mechanized borehole water actors, their operations were governed by the rules of monthly billing based on the metered records of the water consumed. The conditional rule of cash and carry system governed water access towards the maintenance of the water infrastructure. While clients were allowed to fetch water on credit on the occasion of lack of cash at hand grounded in social relations (as neighbours or relatives), continuous default in payment of water service charges was liable for refusal or denial of water services by the concerned actor
The data were then collected from thirty-five (35) non-water service providers through face-to-face interviews using open-ended questions.

The system of monthly billing (when extended via PVC pipes to residents) could not permit access by all residents, due to the inability of low-income residents to finance the cost of networked water extension.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community and household drinking-water service provision and access via non-state water providers (mechanized boreholes with piped PVC extensions, water kiosks, standpipes, wells, tanker trucks, and pushcarts) in three informal settlements of Dar es Salaam where public utility (DAWASA) supply is infrequent.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study directly examines everyday and hybrid governance, institutional arrangements, and formal/informal regulation of urban water infrastructure. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although much of the paper describes self-organized resource mobilization, it also empirically examines specific rule-type mechanisms governing service supply and household access: (1) formal licensing rules (municipal council registration, DAWASA permission, and Ministry of Health operating permits), DAWASA registration of selected tanker trucks, and municipal regulatory discretion/non-enforcement toward unregistered operators treated as a survival strategy; (2) tariff and cost-recovery rules (connection pricing for PVC extensions and metered monthly billing vs. uniform per-litre cash-and-carry pricing); and (3) point-of-service eligibility, accommodation, and enforcement rules (queue exemptions for elders, physically challenged persons, and mothers with infants under one year; barring children under age 10; rationing sales to domestic use during scarcity; discretionary credit based on social relations; and denial of water upon continuous payment default).
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical study based on reconnaissance transect observations (July 2017, follow-up February 2019), snowball sampling to saturation, and open-ended face-to-face interviews in Swahili with 35 non-state water service providers plus the Ubungo municipal water engineer, two Mtaa leaders, and the ward health officer, analysed thematically in MAXQDA.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative outcomes directly relevant to service availability/continuity, affordability-based exclusion from piped connections (low-income residents unable to finance PVC network extensions and metered monthly billing), reliance on kiosks/wells/expensive tanker water due to infrequent DAWASA supply, and conditional access or service denial for continuous payment default (while noting that provider interviews rather than a household survey were conducted).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the study population and sample (35 non-state water operators plus 4 local officials/leaders across 3 informal settlements in Goba ward, Dar es Salaam; provider/settlement unit of analysis), the regulatory/tariff/access-rule mechanisms, qualitative service availability and exclusion outcomes, and qualitative case-study design.

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study (reconnaissance transect walks, snowball sampling, and open-ended face-to-face interviews analysed thematically in MAXQDA)
population_and_sample: 35 non-state water service providers (mechanized borehole distributors, water kiosk operators, well water operator, tap/standpipe operators, tanker truck and pushcart operators) plus the Ubungo municipal water engineer, two Mtaa (ward) leaders, and the ward health officer in three informal settlements (Goba-Chaurembo, Goba-Kibululu, and Goba-Kunguru; 16,491 residents / 3,965 households) in Goba ward, Ubungo Municipality, Dar es Salaam; unit of analysis: non-state water service providers and settlement-level water governance arrangements
exposure: Formal and informal regulatory and operational rules governing non-state water supply and household water access: (1) formal municipal registration, DAWASA permission, and Ministry of Health permitting requirements alongside municipal regulatory forbearance toward unregistered operators and formal DAWASA registration of selected tanker trucks; (2) tariff and cost-recovery rules (upfront PVC pipe connection pricing and metered monthly billing vs. cash-and-carry per-litre pricing); and (3) point-of-access rules governing queue accommodations, child age limits, scarcity rationing to domestic use, social-network credit accommodation, and denial of service for continuous payment default
outcome: Sustained informal water supply availability, affordability-driven exclusion of low-income households from piped PVC extensions and metered monthly billing, household reliance on wells/kiosks/tankers amid infrequent DAWASA supply, and conditional access or denial of water service upon continuous payment default
rationale: This qualitative empirical study in three informal settlements of Dar es Salaam satisfies all inclusion criteria for the systematic review's qualitative mechanism synthesis. Beyond describing grassroots resource mobilization, it empirically documents rule-type mechanisms governing water supply and household access under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2: formal municipal/DAWASA/MoH licensing requirements and street-level municipal forbearance toward unregistered operators, formal DAWASA tanker-truck registration enabling indirect resale through unregistered kiosks, cost-recovery and connection-pricing rules (metered monthly PVC pipe billing vs. cash-and-carry pricing), and unwritten point-of-access rules on queue priority accommodations, scarcity rationing, discretionary credit, and service denial for non-payment. Confidence is rated medium because primary data collection sampled providers and local officials rather than surveying households directly, though qualitative access, exclusion, and service-denial outcomes are explicitly reported.
